newsitem.title: UK: A brief history of the EBRD.
newsitem.headline: A brief history of the EBRD.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) was set up in 1991 to help the former communist countries of central and eastern Europe in the transition to market economies.
The EBRD encourages co-financing and foreign direct investment from the private and public sector in 26 countries.

All powers of the EBRD rest with the Board of Governors, finance ministers from 58 countries and a senior representative from the European Commission and the European Investment Bank. Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn is current chairman of the board.
The board is responsible for operations of the bank and takes decisions on loans and equity investments.
President of the EBRD is former Bank of France governor Jacques de Larosiere. He has not indicated whether he will stay on when his four-year term expires in September.
Following is a brief chronology of the EBRD:

April 1991 - European Bank for Reconstruction and Development founded with headquarters in London. Jacques Attali, president. Eight countries of operation form the initial group -- Albania, Bulgaria, former Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland, Romania, former Soviet Union and former Yugoslavia.
October 1991 - Board approves the three Baltic states -- Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania -- as countries of operation.

1992 - The 12 newly independent states of the former Soviet Union become individual countries of operation. The bank commits funds to 36 projects worth 916 million Ecu in its first full year of operation.
1993 - Attali resigns after an independent audit criticises him for his role in the 66.2 million pound fit-out of London headquarters. Replaced by de Larosiere.
1994 - Three newly independent states from former Yugoslavia -- Croatia, Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia and Slovenia -- become individual countries of operation
1996 - Bosnia and Herzegovina becomes country of operation. 1996 - EBRD secures increase in capital to 20 billion Ecu.
